content: Pneumococcal disease is caused by a type of bacteria known as Streptococcus pneumoniae (commonly referred to as pneumococcus). Individuals with pneumococcal disease can transmit the bacteria to others through respiratory droplets when they cough or sneeze. The pneumococcus bacteria can lead to infections in various parts of the body, including: The lungs, resulting in pneumonia. The ears, causing otitis media. The sinuses, leading to sinusitis. The protective lining of the brain and spinal cord, resulting in meningitis. The bloodstream, causing bacteremia. The symptoms of pneumococcal infection vary depending on the part of the body that is affected. Common symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, stiff neck, confusion, increased sensitivity to light, joint pain, chills, ear pain, sleeplessness, and irritability. In severe cases, pneumococcal disease can result in complications such as hearing loss, brain damage, or even death. Pneumococcal disease occurs worldwide but is more prevalent in lowand middle-income countries where vaccination rates are lower. In regions with four distinct seasons, the disease is more common during the winter and early spring. In tropical climates with distinct dry and rainy seasons, pneumococcal disease tends to occur more frequently during the dry season. Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent pneumococcal disease. Pneumococcal vaccines are routinely recommended in the United States for: Children aged 2 through 18 years who have certain medical conditions. Adults aged 19 years or older who receive the PCV15 vaccine. Some individuals may require multiple doses or booster shots depending on their specific health needs. It is important to consult with your healthcare provider or your child’s clinician to determine the best vaccination plan for your particular situation.
